newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin locks horns with communist-led Duma.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin locks horns with communist-led Duma.

text.p: MOSCOW, April 9 (Russia) - Russian President Boris Yeltsin locked horns with his opponents in parliament on Wednesday, reprimanding the State Duma lower house for the second successive day.

Yeltsin, angered by frequent challenges from the communist-led Duma, accused it of overstepping its constitutional rights by making frequent political judgements on domestic and foreign policy, areas which fall in his domain.

"In 1996 alone the lower house adopted several hundred resolutions containing a political evaluation of the events in the country," Yeltsin said in a letter to Gennady Seleznyov, the Duma's chairman, or speaker.

"It is worth pointing out that most of the documents concerned Russia's domestic and foreign policies, which are the domain of the president under the constitution," said the letter, published by the presidential press service.

The letter followed talks between Yeltsin and Seleznyov on Tuesday where the president said recent legislation had been so badly prepared that he had rejected three out of every four draft laws sent to him.
His scolding coincided with efforts to show a disenchanted public he is putting Russia's house in order and reasserting his authority after an almost eight-month absence with ill-health.
The two sides may be heading for confrontation, but most political experts expect them to flex their muscles rather than enter mortal combat.
Yeltsin said in February he was ready to take on the Duma if necessary, reviving memories of how he dissolved parliament in 1993 and sent tanks to smash hardline deputies into submission.
"They shouldn't attack me too hard because I can hit back," he declared.

Asked at last month's summit with U.S. President Bill Clinton if he could win parliament's approval for agreements, he told reporters: "As far as Russia is concerned, I expect that the State Duma will make a decision based on my advice."
Clinton commented: "Boy, I wish I could give that answer."
But Yeltsin's opponents are smarting from a government reshuffle in which the Kremlin chief promoted liberals including First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, whom the communists hate.
The 450-member Duma, in which the communists are the biggest party but can gain a majority only with the backing of others, has defied Yeltsin on several recent issues.
It voted last week to overturn Yeltsin's veto of a draft law asserting Russian ownership of art treasures seized from Nazi Germany during World War Two.
It also passed a non-binding resolution condemning Yeltsin's suggestion that Soviet state founder Vladimir Lenin's embalmed body be removed from its mausoleum on Red Square and buried.
It has challenged efforts to restructure state monopolies and signalled resistence to proposals for spending cuts, which ministers see as the only way to offset dismal tax revenues.
A row here could last for months, holding up a revised budget for 1997, jeopardising international credits and threatening economic reforms.
But independent politicians say the communists fear losing their domination of the Duma if they push Yeltsin so far as to force him to dissolve the chamber and call a new election.
As the biggest party in the Duma, the communists are to an extent courted by the Kremlin. Often-denied rumours abound of secret deals between the communists and the government.

The Duma has already avoided confrontation on several occasions. It passed the 1997 budget, dropped half-hearted efforts to oust Yeltsin on health grounds and its demands for a vote of no-confidence in the government have repeatedly got nowhere.
Ultra-nationalists have ranted against Yeltsin but then failed to back motions hostile to him or the government.

Yeltsin also has reason for restraint. Antagonising the Duma too much could provoke them to hold up legislation for months and delay reforms, while a new election would be prohibitively costly and could also set back reforms.
